title: Transformers and magnetism
where: the Electrical shelf's Electrical principles folder
folderRuns: AC circuits, Electronics and power electronics, Transformers and magnetism
blurb: Electromagnetism from first principles, then the transformer: turns ratio, losses, regulation, vector groups and stepping 440 V down to 115 V.
from: Brilliant's electricity and magnetism course on brilliant.org (whichever is reachable)
others: Hughes Electrical and Electronic Technology and Bird's Electrical Circuit Theory and Technology (electromagnetism and transformer chapters, contents), OpenStax University Physics volume 2 (magnetism and induction), Khan Academy physics, the Electrical Installation Guide (Schneider) on transformers, and public transformer manufacturers' guides (ABB, Siemens, Schneider) on losses, vector groups and paralleling
syllabi: What a marine electrical engineer actually uses of this topic: the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) and A-III/1 competence lines that touch it, the MCA electro-technical officer and engineer officer syllabus lines (Electrotechnology), the public apprenticeship standards for an electrical or marine engineering technician on the Institute for Apprenticeships site, and the Pearson BTEC HN units that cover it. Exact lines. Also what Dan's BTEC and electrical qualifications covered of magnetism and transformers, so the course moves fast through that
later: Generators and paralleling (built next: it owns the alternator, AVR, governor, synchronising and load sharing)
scope: Magnetism and transformers from first principles, in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) magnetic fields from current: the field round a conductor and a coil, flux and flux density, the right-hand grip; (2) magnetic circuits: magnetomotive force, reluctance, the B-H curve, saturation and hysteresis, and why cores are laminated iron (AC circuits built inductance: go deeper, not over); (3) Faraday's and Lenz's laws: EMF from changing flux, the EMF equation E = 4.44 f N Φ, and why a transformer needs AC; (4) the ideal transformer: turns ratio for voltage and current, power in equals power out, referred impedance; (5) the real transformer: magnetising current, iron losses (hysteresis and eddy currents) and copper losses, the equivalent circuit, open- and short-circuit tests, efficiency and the load for maximum efficiency; (6) regulation: why the secondary voltage falls under load and more so at lagging power factor (AC circuits built phasors: use them), percentage impedance and fault level; (7) three-phase transformers: star and delta windings, vector groups such as Dyn11 and the phase shift they give (Complex numbers built the rotation: use it), and the conditions for paralleling; (8) transformers in service: inrush current, instrument transformers (CTs and VTs, and why a CT secondary must never be opened on load), isolating and auto-transformers, and a general 440 V to 115 V supply as the worked example. Examples from public, general marine and industrial equipment only; never how the Royal Navy or a particular boat does it, never submarine systems beyond CLAUDE.md's public outline, and never anything from Dan's SMQ books.
